newsitem.title: GERMANY: Holzmann plans sweeping series of cutbacks.
newsitem.headline: Holzmann plans sweeping series of cutbacks.

text.p: Troubled German construction company Philipp Holzmann AG to swing back into the black with a sustained programme of cut-backs and sell-offs, Holzmann said in an interview with Germany's Boersen Zeitung.

Holzmann's management board chairman Lothar Mayer and its new chief financial officer Rainer Klee told the paper on Saturday that the group planned to dispose of property holdings worth two billion marks.
To this end, the group said it had found a buyer for its portfolio of 4,000 apartments. The company would not comment on how much Holzmann stood to make from the sale.
Mayer said in the report that as well as thinning out costs, the group would be focusing on cutting the company's debt by billions of marks.
In 1995, Holzmann's net debt stood at six billion marks. Mayer said that this needed to be pared back by a third, and the big property sell-off was the first stage in this process.

The programme of cutbacks, which Meyer described as "healing from within," would continue until the end of 1997 and that the group hoped to be reporting operating profit from the beginning of 1998, Mayer said.

A spokesman for Holzmann told Reuters that the proceeds of the property sale would for the most part counteract any negative effect on earnings from the group's restructuring programme, once this was combined with additional funding from dissolving hidden reserves.
Holzmann made losses of 443 million marks in 1995 following huge write-downs for losses on real estate projects.

The company further denied rumours of liquidity problems at the group as pure fantasy, saying the group had plenty of liquid means at its disposal, which will improve through the sale of the apartments.
The big clean-out of the group's portfolio would also include the sale of subsidiaries in as far as this was possible within the consolidated group.
Holzmann said there were a number of restructuring teams in place trying to bring the ten worst cases among 26 problem units up to speed.

Mayer said he was ready for talks with the construction company Hochtief AG, Holzmann's largest shareholder, whose planned, hostile takeover of Holzmann is still dependent on the word of the Berlin cartel office.
"It is definitely possible that we can cooperate more, especially on contracts abroad," Mayer said.
